Tap it to open your period setup and change the budget, dates or how it is split. Swipe sideways to flip between what is left today and what is left for the whole period. Hold it to see exactly how that number was worked out.

Rest your hand over the top of the screen, near the earpiece, for about a second and every amount blurs out. Cover it again to bring them back.

Start the amount with + to put money back into this period, such as a payday, a refund or a transfer in. Start it with - to take money off. The other keys work as a plain calculator for the amount itself.
Mark the expense as paid by credit card. It still counts against this period, but Minus tracks what you owe separately so you can settle it before your cutoff date.
What you have spent and what is left in the current period, including anything still owed on a credit card.
Tap an expense to expand it and see the full detail. Swipe it right to edit the amount, date, category or note; swipe it left to delete it, with a few seconds to undo.
Recurring charges due in this period sit here before they are paid. Mark one as paid when it lands, or delete just that occurrence to skip it this time without cancelling the series.
Expenses from the period before this one, kept out of the way. Turn this section off again in Settings, under Feature Lab.
Everything that repeats, with what it costs you per period. Open it to see the next due date for each one, or to stop a series you no longer pay.
Anything you logged with a leading + — a payday, a refund, a transfer in. It is added to this period instead of counting as a spend, so your remaining budget goes up.

How to read and write Minus data from an external script

Minus can keep a CSV copy of its data in a folder you pick, and import CSV files you drop into that same folder. External tools get read and write access without touching the database directly.\n\nThe private database stays the source of truth. The folder holds a CSV mirror, not the database file.

Pick a folder above. Minus syncs every two hours from then on, and nothing in the folder is ever deleted except its own old backups.

Each run imports first, then exports, so the file you read always reflects what you just pushed.

1. Imports every file named minus_import_*.csv, renaming each to .imported or .rejected once it has been read.
2. Writes minus_synced.csv, keeping the previous five exports beside it as dated minus_backup- copies.

Android batches background work during Doze and the scheduling floor is 15 minutes, so two hours is a target rather than a guarantee. Use the manual trigger when you need it now.

Replace the folder path with the one you picked. The command above already names the package this build installs as, so it works whether you are running a release or a beta.

The trigger brings the app to the foreground; there is no headless variant. It carries no file path or URI, only telling the app to scan the folder you already granted, so it needs no storage permission.

You can also point the folder at a Syncthing or Dropbox directory and skip adb entirely.

minus_synced.csv carries the full 26 column header and is rewritten every run. The five previous exports are kept beside it as minus_backup- files stamped with the time they were replaced, so a bad export never leaves you without a copy.

Three kinds of row appear in an export, told apart by the first column:

__META__ is budget settings and the current period. One row, first if present.
__ARCHIVED__ is one row per closed budget period.
A timestamp is a transaction.

A reader that only wants transactions must skip the two marker rows. The current_period_id value in the __META__ row is what you echo back in period_id when writing new transactions.

If you reinstall and point Minus at a folder that already holds a minus_synced.csv, it restores from that file instead of overwriting it.

Your file must be named minus_import_<anything>.csv. Minus ignores every other file in the folder, so a shared folder stays untouched.\n\nThe parser reads whatever header your file declares and treats every missing column as empty, so you do not need all 26. This is a complete, valid file.

date is required, exactly yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm. Any other shape discards the row.
amount is required, a plain decimal greater than zero. Minus rows are expenses.
category is optional free text, matched by name and created if new. Blank falls back to Uncategorized.
extra_note is optional free text. Good place for the upstream transaction id.
period_id is recommended, copied from current_period_id in the __META__ row. Blank means 0.
id should be left out. A non-zero value overwrites an existing transaction.
is_recurrent is 1 or 0. If 1, set frequency to WEEKLY, BIWEEKLY or MONTHLY.
is_credit is 1 or 0.

Rows the parser rejects are skipped one by one; the rest of the file still imports.

Name inbound files minus_import_*.csv. Anything else is left alone, including minus_synced.csv and the minus_backup- rotations. This is what makes it safe to point the sync at a folder you share with other tools.

Nothing you drop in is deleted. After a file is read it is renamed to .imported, or to .rejected if any of its rows failed to parse, keeping its contents so you can see what went wrong. Neither name is picked up again.

Never write a non-zero id. Rows with id greater than zero replace the transaction holding that id; rows with id blank or zero insert as new. Because the export carries real row ids, re-pushing an unmodified export overwrites rather than duplicates. You cannot use an export as a template for new rows without clearing the id column first.

Set period_id. Totals are computed from dates, so a row with period_id 0 still shows correctly everywhere. The narrower cost is that it is not attributable to a period and survives the cleanup that runs when an archived period is deleted.

Import is not idempotent. Minus inserts every row it reads without checking for an equivalent transaction. The rename after import stops the same file being read twice, but pushing the same rows under a new name will double-count them, so dedup against minus_synced.csv before you write.

Expenses only. Amounts of zero or less are rejected. Income and budget totals live in the __META__ row, and rewriting those triggers a full settings restore, so treat this channel as append-only for transactions.

Map the provider date to date, reformatted to yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm. Map the amount to amount as an absolute value, skipping inflows. Map the provider category, or your own rule, to category, normalizing names or you will accumulate near-duplicates. Put the provider transaction id in extra_note so it stays visible in the app and gives your dedup a stable handle.

A two-hourly loop looks like this:

1. Pull minus_synced.csv.
2. Parse it, skipping the __META__ and __ARCHIVED__ rows, and note current_period_id.
3. Fetch new provider transactions. For each, check whether the pulled file already holds one with the same amount inside your time window, or the same provider id in extra_note.
4. Write the unmatched ones to a minus_import_ file with the four columns above plus period_id.
5. Push the file, then fire the sync trigger.

Step 3 is where dedup has to happen. Minus will not do it for you.
